::: {#nbk-planning-seam-acceleration-jump-reflected-inertia-torque .callout-notebook title="Seam acceleration and torque requests"}
For the registered CSG-25-50 teaching example, reflected rotor inertia is `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.j_reflected_str`. Correcting a `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.delta_omega_str` reference velocity gap in one `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.dt_tick_str` tick asks for `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_step_str` of inertial torque. Datasheet ratings give `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_rated_str` rated continuous and `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_peak_rated_str` repeated peak torque; this one-tick **request** falls below the rated limit. A symmetric $C^2$ velocity blend over `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.t_blend_str` has `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_mean_str` mean and `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_peak_str` peak inertial torque, a `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.reduction_mult_str` peak-request reduction. Total torque still includes load, gravity, friction, and control response; it needs a full peak and thermal check.
:::

     "50 newton-meters"   = PlanningSeamInertia.tau_step_str
     "50-millisecond"     = PlanningSeamInertia.t_blend
     "1.5 newton-meter"   = PlanningSeamInertia.tau_peak_str
     "33.3x"              = PlanningSeamInertia.reduction_mult_str -->

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_reflected_rotor_inertia_torque_knee.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Illustrative one-tick velocity-step request of 50 newton-meters vs. a 50-millisecond C-squared blend with 1.5 newton-meter peak inertial torque."}

*In this inertia model, the $C^2$ blend cuts the peak inertial torque request by 33.3×.*
:::

Output chatter in learned proposals is a related failure. Stochastic sampling can produce successive chunks whose every sample satisfies position and velocity limits while the commanded acceleration reverses sign rapidly, and each reversal asks the drive for a torque reversal, with the current transitions and $I^2R$ heating that follow if the drive tracks it (@sec-body-actuator-limits).[^fn-hw-thermal-derating] The systems engineer budgets that variation as actuator thermal rise and transmission fatigue, not as perceptual roughness; a trajectory that excites structural resonances or exceeds the drive's thermal limits is infeasible however closely its waypoints follow the task. Even a candidate that passes every internal and seam check must still provide for a replacement that never arrives.

[^fn-hw-thermal-derating]: **Actuator Thermal Derating**\index{Actuator thermal derating!physics}: Joule heating ($I^2R$) in the windings raises stator temperature, and past its limit degrades magnet flux and insulation, so motor controllers enforce derating curves that throttle continuous torque. A velocity profile that ignores this governor meets a mid-trajectory current limit and loses tracking.

## Behavior at the Seam {#sec-planning-behavior-seam}

The transition seam between consecutive action chunks is where physical AI systems face their greatest operational vulnerability. If upstream neural inference encounters scheduling delays, bus stalls, or unhandled exceptions, the execution runtime must manage the seam without violating kinodynamic limits or exhausting mechanical stopping clearance.

### The two-tier deadline hierarchy and commitment cutoffs {#sec-planning-two-tier-deadlines}

The periodic chunk lease and the commitment cutoff answer different questions: whether a replacement has renewed tracking authority recently enough, and whether the reserved stop can still begin in time. The planner also uses a soft *blend deadline* ($t_{\mathrm{blend}}$), a scheduling target for a smooth replacement. Missing that target need not end tracking if the current lease and evidence remain valid and a checked replacement can still arrive before the admission cutoff that precedes physical commitment ($t_{\mathrm{commit}}$). The earlier admission cutoff leaves the response interval needed for the matched stopping suffix to begin at commitment, before its reserved clearance is spent.

For the running mug reach, a stalled proposer expires the shared lease `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` after the last admission. The MCU then requests its state-matched fallback; physical onset follows the separately budgeted response delay. All timeout checks use the MCU monotonic clock. The longer-lease comparison isolates the geometric limit: even with tracking evidence continually renewed, the controller must dispatch the matched stop early enough to begin at commitment. A host progress report changes neither cutoff.

### The C$^2$ stopping suffix and effective deceleration penalty {#sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix}

A moving robot carries continuous momentum. If an emergency brake uses an idealized constant-deceleration profile ($a(t) = -a_{\text{brake}}$), the commanded acceleration steps discontinuously from zero to $-a_{\text{brake}}$ at $t_{\mathrm{commit}}$, and steps discontinuously back to zero when velocity reaches zero. This instantaneous switch demands an infinite jerk impulse ($\dddot{q} = \infty$) and an instantaneous step jump in actuator braking torque ($\Delta\tau = J_{\mathrm{eff}} a_{\text{brake}}$). A real drive can only approximate that step. Whether the response loses traction, disturbs the payload, or exceeds structural limits depends on the load and controller, so the worked design chooses an explicitly smooth profile.

For the selected load-compatible stop, the deceleration profile ramps smoothly up and down with $C^2$ continuity. For a cruise entry with position $q(t_{\mathrm{commit}}) = q_c$, cruise speed $v_c > 0$, and zero entry acceleration, a $C^2$ position-and-velocity-matched stop over duration $T$ parameterizes motion via the normalized time variable $u = (t - t_{\mathrm{commit}}) / T \in [0, 1]$:

$$q(u) = q_c + v_c T \left(u - u^3 + \frac{1}{2} u^4\right), \qquad 0 \le u \le 1$$ {#eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix}

Differentiating @eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix with respect to physical time $t$ ($\frac{d}{dt} = \frac{1}{T} \frac{d}{du}$) yields the continuous velocity, acceleration, and jerk profiles:

$$\begin{aligned}
\dot{q}(u) &= v_c \left(1 - 3u^2 + 2u^3\right) \\
\ddot{q}(u) &= -\frac{6 v_c}{T} u(1 - u) \\
\dddot{q}(u) &= -\frac{6 v_c}{T^2} (1 - 2u)
\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-plan-c2-derivatives}

Evaluating the profiles of @eq-plan-c2-derivatives at the boundaries confirms their physical properties:

- At entry ($u = 0$, $t = t_{\mathrm{commit}}$): $q(0) = q_c$, $\dot{q}(0) = v_c$, and $\ddot{q}(0) = 0$. The suffix seamlessly matches steady-state cruise with zero acceleration step.
- At rest ($u = 1$, $t = t_{\mathrm{commit}} + T$): $q(1) = q_c + \frac{1}{2} v_c T$, $\dot{q}(1) = 0$, and $\ddot{q}(1) = 0$. The mechanism reaches a complete, stable standstill with zero residual acceleration shock.

The deceleration profile $\ddot{q}(u)$ forms a symmetric inverted parabola over $u \in [0, 1]$. Its maximum deceleration occurs at the maneuver midpoint $u = 0.5$ (where $u(1-u) = 1/4$):

$$a_{\mathrm{peak}} = \max_{u \in [0, 1]} |\ddot{q}(u)| = \frac{6 v_c}{T} \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1.5 v_c}{T}$$

Holding the peak at the robot's physical braking limit $a_{\mathrm{peak}} \le a_{\mathrm{brake}}$ fixes the required stopping duration:

$$T = \frac{1.5 v_c}{a_{\mathrm{brake}}}$$

The total stopping distance traveled during the suffix is the integral of velocity over $[0, T]$:

$$d_{C^2} = q(1) - q(0) = \frac{1}{2} v_c T = \frac{1}{2} v_c \left(\frac{1.5 v_c}{a_{\mathrm{brake}}}\right) = \frac{3}{4} \frac{v_c^2}{a_{\mathrm{brake}}} = 1.5 \left(\frac{v_c^2}{2 a_{\mathrm{brake}}}\right)$$

For this cruise-entry profile, the 50 percent increase in braking distance is the **Kinematic Deceleration Tax**: the selected smooth stop costs $1.5\times$ the distance of an idealized constant-deceleration step ($d_{C^2} = 0.75 \frac{v_c^2}{a_{\mathrm{brake}}}$ vs. $0.5 \frac{v_c^2}{a_{\text{brake}}}$). In this stopping budget, the suffix behaves like constant braking at $a_{\text{eff}}=a_{\text{brake}}/1.5$. The factor belongs to the profile just derived, rather than to every smooth stop. Using the constant-deceleration distance without accounting for this profile would understate the required clearance. A nonzero measured entry acceleration requires a general quintic matching the actual $(q,\dot q,\ddot q)$ at entry and zero terminal velocity and acceleration; the permission path checks its interior speed, acceleration, jerk, torque, and clearance.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-c2-stop-clearance
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ C2 STOP SUFFIX ON THE WAREHOUSE MOBILE MANIPULATOR
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-behavior-seam (arm case, base budget row, commitment
# │          counterfactual, checkpoint), @sec-planning-summary.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the C2 suffix for the arm and the base and add its term to the
# │          base's stopping budget.
# │ Show:    Arm 150 mm suffix and 90 mm margin; a lease run 200 ms past
# │          commitment breaches the 300 mm clearance by 110 mm; base
# │          1125 ms / 843.75 mm at 1.5 m/s, +281.25 mm, running total
# │          1194.15 mm past 1.10 m.
# │ How:     RM/AISLE registry fields; calc_c2_stop_suffix for each suffix;
# │          calc_safe_stopping_distance with a_brake (Ch8 total) and with
# │          a_eff = a_brake/1.5 (Ch11 total).
# │
# │ Note:    No aisle-speed value appears here; @sec-enforcement owns the
# │          candidate-speed calculation and outstanding qualification budget.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg, millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PlanningC2Stop:
    """C2 stop suffix for the machine's arm and base, and the budget row it adds."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    # Arm: free-space stop from the machine's TCP speed limit.
    v_arm = RM.tcp_speed_limit  # category: chosen; registry
    t_blend = PlanningArmTimeline.t_blend  # category: chosen; calc-planning-arm-timeline
    t_commit = PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit  # category: chosen
    t_plan_exp = PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp  # category: derived
    t_arm_stop = PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop  # category: illustrative
    d_arm_clear = PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear  # category: illustrative; obstacle clearance, calc-planning-lease-rule
    t_wait = 200 * millisecond  # category: illustrative; tracking authority run past commitment
    # Base: the stop at the rack end.
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative; registry drive limit
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative; credible deceleration, loaded, dry floor
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived; total pre-brake delay
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative; rack-end clear distance

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    a_arm_peak = (1.5 * v_arm / t_arm_stop).to(ureg.meter / ureg.second**2)
    arm_suffix = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_arm, a_arm_peak)
    arm_cruise = (v_arm * (t_commit - t_blend)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    arm_stop_dist = arm_suffix["distance"].to(ureg.millimeter)
    arm_total = arm_cruise + arm_stop_dist
    arm_margin = d_arm_clear - arm_total
    t_stop_end = (t_commit + arm_suffix["duration"]).to(millisecond)
    late_cruise_arm = (v_arm * t_wait).to(ureg.millimeter)
    late_breach_arm = late_cruise_arm - arm_margin

    c2_drive = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_drive, a_brake)
    brake_const = (v_drive**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    c2_increment = c2_drive["distance"].to(ureg.millimeter) - brake_const
    total_prev = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v_drive, tau_delay, a_brake, delta_loc, delta_margin).to(ureg.millimeter)
    total_new = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v_drive, tau_delay, a_brake / 1.5, delta_loc, delta_margin).to(ureg.millimeter)
    excess = total_new - d_clear.to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(a_arm_peak.magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9, "arm suffix peak changed")
    check(abs(arm_suffix["duration"].to(millisecond).magnitude - 300.0) < 1e-9, "arm suffix duration changed")
    check(abs(arm_stop_dist.magnitude - 150.0) < 1e-9, "arm suffix distance changed")
    check(abs(arm_cruise.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "arm pre-onset cruise changed")
    check(abs(arm_margin.magnitude - 90.0) < 1e-9, "arm clearance margin changed")
    check(abs(t_stop_end.magnitude - 600.0) < 1e-9, "arm stop end changed")
    check(t_stop_end == PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_end, "C2 arm stop end disagrees with the timeline cell")
    check(t_blend < t_commit < t_plan_exp < t_stop_end, "arm deadline order broken")
    check(
        abs(arm_stop_dist.magnitude - PlanningLeaseRule.arm_stop_dist.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-9,
        "arm stop disagrees with the lease-rule cell",
    )
    check(
        abs(arm_margin.magnitude - PlanningLeaseRule.commit_margin.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-9,
        "arm margin disagrees with the lease-rule cell",
    )
    check(abs(late_cruise_arm.magnitude - 200.0) < 1e-9, "late-commitment arm cruise changed")
    check(abs(late_breach_arm.magnitude - 110.0) < 1e-9, "late-commitment arm breach changed")
    check(abs(c2_drive["duration"].to(millisecond).magnitude - 1125.0) < 1e-9, "C2 duration at drive limit changed")
    check(abs(c2_drive["distance"].to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 843.75) < 1e-9, "C2 distance at drive limit changed")
    check(abs(brake_const.magnitude - 562.5) < 1e-9, "constant-deceleration braking changed")
    check(abs(c2_increment.magnitude - 281.25) < 1e-9, "C2 budget increment changed")
    check(abs(total_prev.magnitude - 912.9) < 5e-3, "Ch8 running total changed")
    check(abs(total_new.magnitude - 1194.15) < 5e-3, "Ch11 running total changed")
    check(abs(excess.magnitude - 94.15) < 5e-3, "excess over clear distance changed")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    v_arm_str = fmt_velocity(v_arm)
    t_blend_str = fmt_latency(t_blend, unit=millisecond)
    t_commit_str = fmt_latency(t_commit, unit=millisecond)
    t_plan_exp_str = fmt_latency(t_plan_exp, unit=millisecond)
    t_stop_end_str = fmt_latency(t_stop_end, unit=millisecond)
    t_arm_stop_str = fmt_latency(t_arm_stop, unit=millisecond)
    a_arm_peak_str = fmt_acceleration(a_arm_peak)
    arm_stop_dist_str = fmt_length(arm_stop_dist, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    arm_cruise_str = fmt_length(arm_cruise, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    arm_total_str = fmt_length(arm_total, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    arm_margin_str = fmt_length(arm_margin, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    d_arm_clear_str = fmt_length(d_arm_clear, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    v_drive_str = fmt_velocity(v_drive)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake)
    c2_drive_time_str = fmt_latency(c2_drive["duration"], unit=millisecond, commas=True)
    c2_drive_dist_str = fmt_length(c2_drive["distance"], unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    brake_const_str = fmt_length(brake_const, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    c2_increment_str = fmt_length(c2_increment, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    total_prev_str = fmt_length(total_prev, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    total_new_str = fmt_length(total_new, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    excess_str = fmt_length(excess, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    t_wait_str = fmt_latency(t_wait, unit=millisecond)
    late_cruise_arm_str = fmt_length(late_cruise_arm, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    late_breach_arm_str = fmt_length(late_breach_arm, unit=ureg.millimeter)
```

In the alternate longer-lease arm case, the blend deadline is `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_blend_str`, matched commitment `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_commit_str`, nominal setpoint end `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_plan_exp_str`, and stop end `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_stop_end_str`, so $T$ is `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_arm_stop_str`. At the arm's `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_arm_str` Tool Center Point (TCP) speed limit, the suffix's peak deceleration is `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_arm_peak_str` and it travels `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_stop_dist_str`. Clearance is last checked at the blend deadline, so the cruise from `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_blend_str` to physical brake onset at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_commit_str` is charged against that clearance and uses `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_cruise_str`; the full `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_total_str` leaves `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_margin_str` of the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_arm_clear_str` obstacle clearance. Sensing and model error must still come out of that geometric margin. The stated `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_commit_str` is **physical suffix onset**, so the MCU must close replacement admission and pretrigger any communication or actuator delay $\delta$ by that instant minus $\delta$. If it does not, add $v_c\delta$ of travel and shift the stop end; the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_margin_str` margin is then smaller. Nominal setpoints end at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_plan_exp_str` while MCU STOP continues to `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_stop_end_str`, and the case assumes that fresh target evidence keeps TRACK valid until stop dispatch (@sec-planning-goal-to-trajectory).

A stall on this machine never reaches commitment. One permission tick, one bus cycle, and brake onset, `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_dispatch_str` together, put the arm's stop onset `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_path_str` after the last admission, or `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_lease_path_str` of travel at the TCP limit. From zero-acceleration cruise the $C^2$ profile matches the arm at whatever instant it starts, so the state-matched fallback travels the same `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.arm_stop_dist_str` as the matched stop suffix. The renewal-to-onset path therefore uses `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.lease_total_str` of the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear_str` clearance and leaves `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.lease_margin_str`. The alternate schedule leaves `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.commit_margin_str` measured from its later clearance check; the two margins have different evidence epochs. The `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` alternate admission cutoff is an absolute schedule offset; it is not a maximum lease duration justified by the running case's clearance at admission. That lease must fit its own evidence age, response travel, stop, and uncertainty reserve.

In the alternate arm schedule, commitment preserves the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_margin_str` margin computed from clearance dated at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_blend_str`. Missing the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` admission cutoff and delaying stop dispatch by `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_wait_str` would delay physical stop onset that far past commitment, and cruise at the TCP limit would add `{python} PlanningC2Stop.late_cruise_arm_str` before the same stop and breach the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_arm_clear_str` clearance by `{python} PlanningC2Stop.late_breach_arm_str`. A later stop must still match its actual entry state; this counterfactual holds cruise speed constant only to show the lost clearance. An arm that waits that long may already occupy a state from which no admissible control avoids the obstacle.

### Inevitable collision states and physical commitment boundaries {#sec-planning-inevitable-collision-states}

In classical robotic path planning, obstacle avoidance was frequently treated as a static geometric query: does the robot's physical configuration intersect an obstacle volume at the current instant? In physical AI systems operating with continuous momentum, this static spatial check is dangerously inadequate. A mobile manipulator moving with high velocity and finite actuator braking torque cannot reverse its direction or halt instantaneously. Long before the machine physically touches an obstacle, its combined dynamic state—position, velocity, acceleration, and traction limits—can cross an irreversible boundary beyond which every mathematically possible control trajectory leads inevitably to collision. In dynamic systems and control theory, such states are classified as Inevitable Collision States (ICS).

The commitment deadline $t_{\mathrm{commit}}$ and the certified stopping suffix are co-designed precisely so that the machine initiates braking *before* its dynamic state enters an Inevitable Collision State $\text{ICS}(\mathcal{X}_{\text{obs}})$. If an action chunk's stopping suffix requires distance $d_{\text{stop}} > d_{\text{clear}}$, that suffix cannot justify admitting the chunk. Failure of this particular stop does not establish that every admissible maneuver collides, as the definition of an inevitable collision state requires. The architecture nevertheless refuses the proposal because it lacks the independently executable stop on which its permission depends. The safety microcontroller therefore enforces the hard admission invariant:
$$d_{\text{stop}}(t_{\mathrm{commit}}) \le d_{\text{clear}}(t_{\mathrm{commit}})$$
If the controller delays braking past commitment in the hope that an overdue neural replanner will deliver an evasive path, physical momentum can carry the machine into an ICS from which no admissible control input can prevent impact.

::: {#dfn-planning-inevitable-collision-state .callout-definition title="Inevitable collision state"}

***Inevitable collision state***\index{Inevitable collision state!definition}\index{Collision avoidance!inevitable collision state} (ICS) is any dynamic plant state $\mathbf{x}(t) \in \mathcal{X}$ from which every physically admissible future control trajectory $\mathbf{u}_{[t, \infty)} \in \mathcal{U}$ inevitably produces collision with an obstacle or constraint boundary:
$$\mathbf{x} \in \text{ICS}(\mathcal{X}_{\text{obs}}) \iff \forall \mathbf{u}(\cdot) \in \mathcal{U}, \; \exists \tau \ge t \text{ such that } \mathbf{x}(\tau) \in \mathcal{X}_{\text{obs}}$$
where $\mathcal{U}$ denotes the admissible control input set bounded by actuator torque, traction, and deceleration limits.

1.  **Significance**: Sets the commitment deadline $t_{\text{commit}}$ in receding-horizon planning; continuing nominal motion past it without an admitted successor can carry the plant into an ICS, and no later replanning can bring it back out.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike static geometric collision checks that evaluate only instantaneous spatial overlap ($\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}_{\text{obs}}$), an ICS identifies dynamically trapped states where current momentum and finite braking torque make future boundary breach physically unavoidable.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Delaying emergency braking in the expectation that an overdue neural planner will complete an evasive path, ignoring that moving mass enters an ICS long before geometric contact occurs.

:::

These deadlines and the stop they protect are fixed at admission, before motion begins. The candidate declares payload, contact, effort, and obstacle assumptions. The MCU first validates its fixed header and lineage, then checks the complete bounded trajectory and suffix, including the seam $(q,\dot q,\ddot q)$ against the reachable state envelope from its current estimate, interior extrema, clearance, stopping distance, and a feasible response from every state reachable through physical stop onset. A scan over $N$ setpoints is $O(N)$, even with a fixed maximum $N$ and measured worst-case execution time; after admission, a distinct $O(1)$ per-tick check reads the current state and local reference. A replacement received after the blend deadline passes the same check with a compressed bridge, whose higher acceleration and torque its extrema must still clear, and if the check cannot finish before the earlier admission cutoff, the MCU retains the current record only while its own lease, evidence, and fallback remain valid. A candidate received after commitment cannot restore the spent runway.

The planner proposes the suffix, but the MCU latches the validated payload and stop coefficients into protected memory **before** enabling TRACK and dispatches that resident path before commitment without reading host DRAM, so a host crash, bus stall, or corrupted shared packet cannot erase the stop.[^fn-hw-dma-pingpong] If the measured state falls outside the latched suffix's entry region, the MCU uses the state-matched fallback; torque disable or a spring brake is not a universal substitute for a controlled stop, especially with a suspended load (@sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder).

[^fn-hw-dma-pingpong]: **Inter-core shared-memory contracts**\index{Inter-processor communication!shared memory}\index{Real-time systems!memory barriers}: A shared-memory implementation needs an ownership protocol, cache maintenance where required, and release/acquire ordering. The MCU validates a completed candidate and copies the admitted plan and stop into protected memory before activation.

### Base stopping budget inflation under gentle deceleration {#sec-planning-base-stopping-budget}

The base of the mobile manipulator stops the same way, and for a reason of its own. The loaded tote rack tolerates the machine's credible deceleration only if that deceleration is reached gradually; the selected polynomial stop costs half again the distance of constant-deceleration braking at the same peak. That cost now enters the stopping budget. At the drive limit of `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_drive_str`, a suffix that peaks at the credible `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_brake_str` lasts `{python} PlanningC2Stop.c2_drive_time_str` and travels `{python} PlanningC2Stop.c2_drive_dist_str`, against the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.brake_const_str` of constant-deceleration braking in @eq-body-stopping-distance. The suffix therefore adds `{python} PlanningC2Stop.c2_increment_str` to the budget that @sec-perception-transduction-calibration left at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.total_prev_str`, for a running total of `{python} PlanningC2Stop.total_new_str`. That partial total already passes the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_clear_str` rack-end clear distance by `{python} PlanningC2Stop.excess_str`. It inherits the earlier delay ledger's still-unqualified dispatch-to-admission interval; adding that interval can only increase the stopping requirement. The calculation is a conditional design deficit, not a measured complete response bound.

This `{python} PlanningC2Stop.excess_str` deficit proves that the robot cannot safely cruise at its `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_drive_str` drive limit in this aisle once smooth, non-destructive stopping kinetics are respected. The machine must either derate its maximum operating speed or expand its perception horizon. This intentional deficit sets up the runtime enforcement speed governor in @sec-enforcement. This is the stopping condition of Principle \ref{pri-vol4-irreversibility} with one more term, because a stop the load can tolerate is a longer stop and the distance it adds comes out of the same clear distance. This calculation concerns the fixed rack-end boundary. A person entering the aisle requires separately qualified moving-actor bounds and crossing control or an operating restriction, as discussed in @sec-memory; this static clearance ledger does not establish that protection. Under the selected body and aisle constraints, reducing speed can recover clearance. @Sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes adds the tracking allowance and derives a candidate speed; permission to operate still requires complete capture-to-admission timing, positive stopping reserve, and qualification under the declared conditions.

For either body, the admission and fallback decisions in @tbl-11-seam-fallback-hierarchy are distinct from an emergency power cut.

| State                      | Trigger                                                                                           | MCU action and required evidence                                                                                                                             |
|:---------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| TRACK, ordinary handoff    | Replacement passes the complete admission check before the admission cutoff preceding commitment. | Latch the new nominal path and its own stop, then transfer at a checked $C^2$ seam.                                                                          |
| TRACK, late candidate      | Candidate arrives after the blend deadline but before the admission cutoff preceding commitment.  | Admit only if the compressed bridge, full path, stop, and timing still fit; otherwise retain the current record only while its own permission remains valid. |
| STOP, matched suffix       | No successor admitted by the earlier cutoff.                                                      | MCU follows its protected suffix from the validated entry state; nominal tracking may end while STOP continues.                                              |
| STOP, earlier invalidation | Lease lapse, intent expiry, contact, state mismatch, or fault before physical stop onset.         | MCU selects the state-matched fallback with reserved clearance.                                                                                              |
| Fault response             | Controlled stop cannot be assured from measured state.                                            | Use the machine-specific risk response (which may include drive inhibit, brake, or compliance) only under its validated load and timing assumptions.         |

: **Tracking and fallback decisions**: A host crash does not remove a latched stop. TRACK is the nominal mode; STOP is the stop rung of the fallback ladder in @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder. {#tbl-11-seam-fallback-hierarchy tbl-colwidths="[18,29,53]"}

::: {#chk-plan-fallback-clearance-stopping-budget .callout-checkpoint title="Commitment and full stopping clearance"}

Before committing an autonomous machine to an action chunk, verify your understanding of commitment deadlines, stopping budgets, and trajectory continuity:

- [ ] **Deadline distinction**: Can you distinguish nominal setpoint end, physical stop completion, and target-evidence expiry?
- [ ] **Continuous entry**: Why would a constant-deceleration switch fail $C^2$ matching at zero-acceleration cruise entry?
- [ ] **Clearance and latency**: The arm's `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_margin_str` margin already charges cruise from the blend deadline to commitment. Where must an unreserved delay $\delta$ beyond it be charged, and how much of that margin does $v_c\delta$ consume?

:::

The mug reach now has a complete execution argument: a timed prefix, a checked seam, and a stop reserved under stated conditions. These obligations let us compare trajectory generators by the candidate work they perform rather than by treating their outputs as permission.

## Choosing a Trajectory Generator {#sec-planning-paradigms}

The mug reach now has an execution requirement: each admitted prefix must join the current state and preserve a feasible stop. Choosing a route around the conveyor guard and choosing how quickly to follow that route remain separate decisions. Geometric search addresses the route; continuous optimization assigns or adjusts motion under constraints. Learned action chunking can propose motion directly from observations, but its output still needs both checks.

Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM) [@kavraki1996probabilistic] reuse a sampled configuration-space roadmap across queries, while Rapidly-exploring Random Trees (RRT, RRT*) [@lavalle1998rapidly] grow a search tree from the start configuration; RRT* rewires connections to improve path cost. These methods help choose a route through obstacle geometry. A geometric route still needs time parameterization, smooth joins, actuator-limit checks, and a stopping continuation before the moving arm can follow it. Search resolves where motion can go; trajectory synthesis must determine how the body can traverse that route.

The complementary classical lens is **constrained continuous trajectory optimization**, exemplified by Covariant Hamiltonian Optimization for Motion Planning (CHOMP), Trajectory Optimization for Motion Planning (TrajOpt), Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP), and receding-horizon Model Predictive Control (MPC) [@tedrake2023manipulation; @lynch2017modern]. Rather than sampling discrete graph nodes, continuous trajectory optimization parameterizes motion as a time-indexed curve $\mathbf{q}(t)$ and minimizes an objective functional balancing dynamic smoothness against obstacle proximity:

$$\min_{\mathbf{q}(t)} \quad \mathcal{U}[\mathbf{q}] = \int_0^T \left( \frac{1}{2} \|\dddot{\mathbf{q}}(t)\|^2 + \lambda_{\text{obs}} c_{\text{obs}}(\mathbf{q}(t)) \right) dt$$

subject to physical boundary conditions and actuator invariants:
$$\mathbf{q}(0) = \mathbf{q}_0, \quad \dot{\mathbf{q}}(0) = \dot{\mathbf{q}}_0, \quad \ddot{\mathbf{q}}(0) = \ddot{\mathbf{q}}_0$$
$$\mathbf{q}(T) = \mathbf{q}_{\text{goal}}, \quad \dot{\mathbf{q}}(T) = \mathbf{0}, \quad \ddot{\mathbf{q}}(T) = \mathbf{0}$$
$$|\dot{\mathbf{q}}(t)| \le \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\max}, \quad |\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q})| \le \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\max}$$

Continuous optimization adjusts motion within a chosen route, but non-convex obstacle geometry can trap a local solver in a dead-end pocket. Geometric search can supply an alternative route; a learned proposal can supply one from visual observations. Neither removes the need to check the resulting timed motion against the model and actuator limits.

Repeatedly replanning from an updated state is the structure of classical **Model Predictive Control (MPC)**\index{Model Predictive Control!receding horizon}\index{Trajectory optimization!collocation and MPC} and trajectory optimization, where an optimizer plans a trajectory over a finite horizon $T$, executes an initial prefix, and resolves the problem from the updated state on the next cycle. The cost ranks candidate motions; the constraints rule out motions the model cannot execute safely. Classical MPC expresses these two jobs as a constrained numerical optimization problem over discrete steps $k = 0, \dots, N-1$ [@tedrake2023manipulation; @lynch2017modern]:

$$\begin{aligned}
\min_{\mathbf{u}_{0:N-1}} \quad & \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \ell(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) + \ell_f(\mathbf{x}_N) \\
\text{subject to} \quad & \mathbf{x}_{k+1} = f(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k), \quad k = 0, \dots, N-1 \\
& \mathbf{x}_k \in \mathcal{X}_{\text{safe}}, \quad \mathbf{u}_k \in \mathcal{U}_{\text{adm}}, \quad k = 0, \dots, N-1 \\
& \mathbf{x}_N \in \mathcal{X}_f
\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-plan-mpc-formulation}

The variables in @eq-plan-mpc-formulation separate predicted state from chosen input: the model advances the state at each step, and every predicted step must remain admissible. The stage cost $\ell(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k)$ penalizes tracking error and control effort, while the safe state set $\mathcal{X}_{\text{safe}}$ enforces collision-free clearances obtained from the Scene Memory State (Contract 8), and the admissible control set $\mathcal{U}_{\text{adm}}$ enforces joint torque and voltage limits from the body's Limit Record. The terminal constraint places the final state in a **terminal invariant set**, $\mathbf{x}_N \in \mathcal{X}_f$. In control theory, *recursive feasibility* (the mathematical guarantee that if a feasible trajectory exists at time $t$, a feasible solution is guaranteed to exist at $t+1$) can be established under suitable model and constraint assumptions by requiring that the terminal state $\mathbf{x}_N$ lands within a region where a known, safe control law keeps the system safe indefinitely. For this architecture, the terminal condition requires a validated braking continuation that brings the machine to rest within observed clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$). That finite stop is not by itself an indefinitely invariant set: moving obstacles can enter the stopped machine’s space unless the environment or crossing controls preserve clearance.

Continuous-time optimal control problems are typically transcribed into finite-dimensional non-linear programs via **direct shooting** (forward-integrating controls) or **direct collocation**[^fn-plan-collocation-defects] (parameterizing states and controls with polynomial splines and enforcing dynamic defect constraints $f(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) - \dot{\mathbf{x}}_k = \mathbf{0}$ at interior knots). MPC guarantees depend on the model, constraints, terminal conditions, and timely solution. Contact changes can make the numerical problem difficult to solve before the deadline. Learned chunking avoids solving that optimization during each prediction, but does not enforce the terminal invariant constraint $\mathbf{x}_N \in \mathcal{X}_f$; a predicted chunk can end where the machine lacks room to stop.

[^fn-plan-collocation-defects]: **Direct Collocation Defects in Real-Time Solvers**\index{Direct collocation!defect constraints}: Direct collocation converts continuous-time control problems into finite Non-Linear Programs (NLPs) by enforcing dynamic defect constraints $\Delta_k = \dot{\mathbf{x}}(t_k) - f(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) = \mathbf{0}$ at quadrature points. When contact transitions or unmodeled friction introduce non-smooth gradients, NLP solver convergence degrades from quadratic Newton rates to slow line searches, causing real-time control deadlines to be missed.

A learned proposer and a constrained trajectory generator can divide these jobs. The proposer supplies motion alternatives from observations; the generator adjusts a candidate to satisfy boundary, actuator, and clearance constraints. This adjustment can fail or miss its deadline, so it remains on the proposal side of the independent admission check.

Mathematically, this dual-stage pipeline formulates trajectory generation as a constrained projection operator $\Pi_{\mathcal{K}}(\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{learned}})$:

$$\mathbf{q}^*(t) = \Pi_{\mathcal{K}}(\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{learned}}) = \arg\min_{\mathbf{q}(t)} \int_0^T \|\mathbf{q}(t) - \hat{\mathbf{q}}_{\text{learned}}(t)\|_{\mathbf{W}_q}^2 dt + \int_0^T \|\dddot{\mathbf{q}}(t)\|_{\mathbf{W}_j}^2 dt$$ {#eq-plan-kinodynamic-projection}

subject to physical boundary conditions and safety invariants across the execution interval $t \in [0, T]$:
$$\mathbf{q}(0) = \mathbf{q}_{\text{actual}}, \quad \dot{\mathbf{q}}(0) = \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\text{actual}}, \quad \ddot{\mathbf{q}}(0) = \ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{\text{actual}}$$
$$\mathbf{q}(t) \in \mathcal{C}_{\text{free}}, \quad |\dot{\mathbf{q}}(t)| \le \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\max}, \quad |\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q})| \le \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\max}$$
$$d_{\text{stop}}(\mathbf{q}(t_{\text{commit}}), \dot{\mathbf{q}}(t_{\text{commit}})) \le d_{\text{clear}}(t_{\text{commit}})$$

In @eq-plan-kinodynamic-projection, the first term penalizes departure from the learned proposal and the second penalizes jerk. The weighted norm is $\|z\|_W^2=z^T Wz$, with positive semidefinite weights, and $\mathcal{K}$ denotes the trajectories satisfying the displayed constraints. The constraints supply the physical obligations that the prediction alone lacks. A feasible solution is still conditional on the state, load, and obstacle assumptions used by the generator; independent admission checks those assumptions and the resulting motion.

The proposer changes the computation budget, not these obligations. ACT [@zhao2023learning] predicts joint setpoints in one forward pass and ensembles overlapping predictions (@sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline), but coordinate averaging does not match boundary derivatives. Diffusion policies [@chi2024diffusionpolicy] generate alternatives through iterative denoising, adding inference work to the replacement path. A learned warm-start instead supplies candidate knots to a numerical solver; it may reduce iterations, but an unfamiliar input can still lead to an infeasible solution or a missed deadline. Planner selection therefore depends on whether the task needs route exploration, constrained local motion, or proposals from high-dimensional observations, and on the time available to validate the result.

@Tbl-11-planning-paradigms compares the inputs, constraints, and seam obligations of the synthesis methods.

| Trajectory paradigm                         | Input representation                                             | Dynamic and safety guarantees                                       | Dominant workload        | Boundary continuity across replanning                       |
|:--------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| Combinatorial Graph Search (PRM, RRT*)      | Configuration samples $\mathbf{q} \in \mathcal{C}_{\text{free}}$ | Route quality depends on the search; dynamics need separate checks  | Collision queries        | Piecewise-linear ($C^0$); discontinuous $\ddot{\mathbf{q}}$ |
| Classical Numerical MPC                     | Low-dimensional state vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$       | Constraint and stability guarantees depend on model and assumptions | Constrained solve        | Continuity requires explicit boundary constraints           |
| Sampling-Based Optimization (MPPI) | State vector and signed distance fields (ESDF)                   | Constraint treatment depends on the formulation and solver          | Rollouts or optimization | Requires spline smoothing or terminal costs                 |
| Generative Action Chunking (ACT, Diffusion) | High-dimensional multimodal tokens (vision, text)                | Empirical demonstration distribution; zero formal safety guarantees | Model inference          | Discrete samples; requires checked interpolation and seam      |

: **Comparison of trajectory generation paradigms**: Search, optimization, and learned proposals perform different candidate-generation work. Solve time and supported constraints depend on the implementation and problem; every selected pipeline still needs checked dynamics, seams, and stopping clearance. {#tbl-11-planning-paradigms tbl-colwidths="[22,23,23,14,18]"}

The generator choice changes how a candidate is found and how much admission work it creates. It does not change the response to an invalid candidate or a changed world. Those failures must be distinguished because rejecting a replacement need not invalidate the motion already under way.

## Trajectory Planning Failure Modes and Infeasible Seams {#sec-planning-failure-modes}

A replacement for the mug reach can fail in the candidate itself, at its join to the moving arm, or after admission when the world changes. Where the failure first becomes visible determines which subsystem has the evidence to reject the motion and how much time remains to stop. Candidate and boundary checks address the first two cases; runtime monitoring addresses the third.

### Pre-execution limit and boundary checkers {#sec-planning-pre-execution-checkers}

Before any proposed trajectory setpoint can influence actuator registers, the deterministic safety MCU screens the candidate record through two independent admission gates within a measured worst-case time budget. Fixed-degree seam calculations have bounded work per axis; checking a complete setpoint sequence also depends on its length:

1.  **Pre-execution Bound Checker:** Evaluates the proposed neural action chunk in isolation against intrinsic kinematic, dynamic, and stopping invariants across the full candidate horizon $[t_{\mathrm{start}}, t_{\mathrm{plan\_exp}}]$. Beyond testing margin functions $M(t) = L_{\mathrm{limit}} - |x(t)|$ across joint positions $q(t)$, contracted velocity limits $|\dot{q}(t)| \le v_{\max} - \frac{1}{4} a_{\max} T_s$ (@eq-plan-contracted-velocity-limit), and free-space inverse-dynamics joint torques $|\boldsymbol{\tau}(t)| = |\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q})| \le \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{rated}}$, the checker enforces the crucial stopping invariant: the candidate's matched stopping suffix must satisfy $d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$ within observed free space. Any knot or interior interval where $M(t) < 0$ or where stopping runway breaches clearance triggers immediate rejection, logging a diagnostic fault record naming the joint index, timestamp, and negative margin. Crucially, rejection at the admission gate causes no mechanical shudder or physical pause: the tracking controller can continue the previously admitted trajectory only while its own state, evidence, lease, and stopping reserve remain valid. A rejected replacement does not renew that lease.
2.  **Boundary Checker:** Evaluates the transition seam between the currently executing trajectory $A$ and the candidate replacement $B$ at $t_{\mathrm{seam}}$. Because unconstrained sequence decoders predict open-loop action tokens without terminal derivative matching, concatenating raw chunks can leave acceleration steps. At earlier admission it checks the reachable seam-state envelope; at activation, the boundary checker uses encoder-based estimates $(\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{meas}}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\mathrm{meas}}, \ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{\mathrm{meas}})$ and their error bounds, estimates the physical seam gap $(\Delta\mathbf{q}, \Delta\dot{\mathbf{q}}, \Delta\ddot{\mathbf{q}})$, and evaluates whether an analytical $C^2$ quintic bridge (@eq-plan-quintic-spline-matrix) can reconcile the boundary while meeting torque limits and the drive's voltage and current-slew constraints. The one-tick estimate $\tau_{\mathrm{request}} = J_{\mathrm{eff}} \frac{\Delta\dot q}{T_c}$ screens a velocity mismatch; the finite bridge still needs its own interior checks.

For the CSG-25-50 joint of the seam notebook, counting only its `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.j_reflected_str` reflected rotor inertia over one `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.dt_tick_str` tick and allocating the whole `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_peak_rated_str` repeated-peak rating to this acceleration gives an *idealized ceiling* of `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.dq_ceiling_str` on $\Delta\dot q$. Available margin is smaller after link and payload inertia, gravity, friction, other commanded torque, current rise time, and thermal or bus limits are accounted for. The permission path must use that state-dependent margin and the measured drive response when evaluating a finite bridge. It rejects a direct velocity discontinuity even if its one-tick arithmetic falls below that ceiling; a bounded $C^2$ bridge and its interior checks are still required.[^fn-inc-seam-trip]

[^fn-inc-seam-trip]: **Drive and resonance response**\index{Drivetrain!resonant frequency}\index{Inverter!desaturation trip}: A sharp command can excite a joint's *identified* flexible modes, but their frequencies and damping depend on the transmission and load. Current limiting, desaturation detection, DC-bus response, and shutdown depend on the selected driver and its configuration; see the [TI gate-driver protection description](https://www.ti.com/document-viewer/lit/html/SLVAG18/GUID-1263241E-9C90-419F-B3D8-D2F599BCABEA).

### Runtime tracking monitors and unmodeled contact trips {#sec-planning-runtime-monitors}

After admission, a slipping payload or new contact can invalidate the dynamics used to check the plan. Runtime monitoring must detect that change while the remaining clearance still supports a response.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-monitor-trip
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RUNTIME MONITOR TRIP THRESHOLDS FOR THE ARM
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-failure-modes (runtime monitors paragraph).
# │
# │ Goal:    Derive the tool-position error trip from the budgeted clearance and
# │          the deflection allowance, beside the unmodeled-contact threshold.
# │ Show:    0.020 m - 0.005 m = 0.015 m; 10 N contact threshold.
# │ How:     Illustrative clearance, allowance, and contact threshold.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_length, fmt_force

class PlanningMonitorTrip:
    """Position-error trip threshold and contact threshold for the arm."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    d_clearance = 0.020 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative; budgeted clearance past the conveyor guard
    d_deflect = 0.005 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative; payload deflection and gearbox compliance
    f_contact = 10 * ureg.newton  # category: illustrative; unmodeled free-space contact threshold

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    eps_pos = (d_clearance - d_deflect).to(ureg.meter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(eps_pos.magnitude - 0.015) < 1e-12, "position error trip changed")
    check(eps_pos.magnitude > 0, "deflection allowance consumes the clearance")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    d_clearance_str = fmt_length(d_clearance, unit=ureg.meter, precision=3)
    d_deflect_str = fmt_length(d_deflect, unit=ureg.meter, precision=3)
    eps_pos_str = fmt_length(eps_pos, unit=ureg.meter, precision=3)
    f_contact_str = fmt_force(f_contact, precision=0)
```

Independent **runtime monitors**\index{Runtime monitor} detect changed-world infeasibility by observing four dedicated signals, comprising joint state divergence, tracking error velocity, unexpected contact wrenches, and the invalidation of the geometric assumptions the record declares (@sec-planning-trajectory-contract). This derivation demonstrates **Spatial Margin Budgeting**: geometric obstacle clearance cannot be allocated entirely to tracking error. Physical compliance and mechanical deflection under load consume clearance before any tracking divergence occurs. The tracking error allowance $\epsilon_{\mathrm{pos}}$ is therefore the total swept-volume clearance less the structural deflection and gearbox compliance allowance $\delta_{\mathrm{deflect}}$. For the mobile manipulator's arm reaching past the conveyor guard, a budgeted swept-volume clearance of `{python} PlanningMonitorTrip.d_clearance_str` and an unmodeled payload deflection and gearbox compliance allowance $\delta_{\mathrm{deflect}}$ of `{python} PlanningMonitorTrip.d_deflect_str` leave an allowance $\epsilon_{\mathrm{pos}}$ of `{python} PlanningMonitorTrip.eps_pos_str`. This remainder is an upper allocation before post-trip growth and uncertainty reserve, not a usable trip threshold by itself. Detection, dispatch, and actuator-onset travel, the fallback swept motion, and state-estimation uncertainty require separate reserved clearance. The allowance caps the tracking bound rather than replacing it. The arm tracker's own validated bound, the arm's instance of the $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$ that @sec-enforcement-handoff validates for the base, must sit inside those `{python} PlanningMonitorTrip.eps_pos_str`, and the per-tick check trips on $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$. If measured Cartesian tool-position error $\|\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{tool,actual}}(t)-\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{tool,planned}}(t)\|$ exceeds $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$, or a six-axis force-torque sensor reports an unmodeled `{python} PlanningMonitorTrip.f_contact_str` contact in this free-space example, the monitor revokes nominal tracking and requests the validated state-matched fallback. Actual deceleration begins after the measured detection, dispatch, and actuator response delays.

A plan can also exhaust its nominal references before the next candidate passes admission. The MCU must not wait for the execution pointer to run off the array or treat a final-position hold as a stop. On this machine the chunk lease ends the wait first, and the alternate schedule separately enforces the pre-onset admission cutoff of @sec-planning-behavior-seam, which the MCU applies in its own monotonic clock. Complete stopping clearance includes detection, dispatch, actuator response, and motion under the selected profile; an assumed constant deceleration is insufficient for the $C^2$ worked suffix.

Every detector in this section relies on an explicit contract between the trajectory generator and the execution runtime. A plan delivered as a raw list of coordinates, without its valid lifespan, clearance bounds, boundary derivatives, and fallback, leaves the permission path unable to tell whether an ongoing motion remains safe or has drifted into infeasibility.

## The Trajectory Contract {#sec-planning-trajectory-contract}

Each time the chunk policy proposes `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.n_horizon_str` new setpoints for the reach toward the mug, the permission path must decide whether to admit them without asking the planner anything. The formal **Trajectory Plan** record (`TrajectoryRecord`, the tenth contract in the physical AI lineage)\index{Trajectory Plan!contract record}\index{Cyber-physical contract!trajectory planning}, immutable and handed over at every replanning cycle, makes that decision possible. The trajectory record is not merely a data serialization schema or ROS message definition; it is a formal **Cyber-Physical Contract** that enforces physical invariants across the causal boundary.

The record lets the MCU make an admission decision without continuing cooperation from the proposer. It checks the candidate in its staging buffer, validates the bounded trajectory and stopping continuation, and copies the admitted content into protected memory. Complete admission may scan the setpoints; its worst-case duration must fit before the admission cutoff preceding commitment. The separate per-tick check then uses the current state and local reference. A host crash cannot remove the resident stop; executing it still requires available sensing, drive energy, and braking authority, and loss of the chunk lease can trigger fallback before the record reaches commitment.

The inputs established at the planning handoff remain part of its lineage: scene memory supplies geometry and clearance, and intent supplies the target, tolerances, effort ceilings, and parent lease. The completed record passes those assumptions with the motion to @sec-enforcement, where current state determines per-tick permission.

Each field records a reason the motion was admitted. Boundary derivatives establish what the seam must join; deadlines state when nominal motion must yield to stopping; the sidecar identifies the scene and load assumptions under which the checks held. The record preserves those obligations for the execution runtime rather than turning the planner's claimed feasibility into permission.

If the physical plant violates declared bounds—such as payload mass, contact impedance, surface friction, or ODD geometry—the contract is breached, and TRACK authority is revoked immediately by the safety MCU. Admission requires the matched stop suffix to be resident in MCU protected memory and checked within observed clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$) from its commitment entry state. Earlier invalidation requires a feasible state-matched fallback from the measured state, as established in @sec-planning-handoff. The trajectory record answers to the intent lease of @sec-intent-lease, whose digest it carries as its parent, and every setpoint it proposes pursues the lease's target without exceeding its effort ceilings. The record stores the motion as setpoint arrays or spline coefficients, together with the sample cadence (on this machine a `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_period_str` period $\Delta t_{\text{step}}$, a `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.f_step_str` setpoint stream), the nominal end $t_{\mathrm{plan\_exp}}$ (`{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp_str` for one chunk), and SI units. With the frame and evidence time of @sec-planning-handoff, the units, and the cadence in the handoff, the joint controller interpolates setpoints and evaluates derivatives without frame mismatches or reliance on ambient system clocks.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Trajectory feasibility proposals are separately checked against conditional control barrier functions in @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission.
:::

Physical feasibility depends on the scene and load used to validate the plan. The immutable sidecar therefore identifies obstacle-map epochs, payload and friction assumptions, limits, validator version, measured margin, and the source observation, and a digest in the fixed header binds it to the setpoints. The validator proves the stop feasible only under these assumptions, and they may claim no more than evaluation sampled, so the payload and friction the sidecar declares must lie inside the target Operational Design Domain (ODD) of @sec-evaluation-logs. The permission path revokes TRACK when live state leaves them, since a recorded margin holds only for the scene it was computed against. Solver seed and model hash belong in the audit sidecar for reproducibility where the toolchain supports it, not in the servo's per-tick path.

On this machine the chunk policy's output supplies only the nominal part of each trajectory record. Planning adds the seam state, the four deadlines, and the matched stop suffix, so the permission path admits one stream of records. The fixed header groups each record's fields by purpose. Lineage fields give a sequence number, the evidence time $t_0$, and the digest of the parent intent lease. Timing fields give the four deadlines of @sec-planning-handoff, and the record's tracking authority ends at the earliest of its pre-onset stop-dispatch cutoff, the lapse of the chunk lease (@sec-nervous-cadences) `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` after the last admitted chunk, the parent intent's expiry, and target-evidence expiry. Seam fields give the frame, each joint's entry state $(q,\dot q,\ddot q)$, and the certified stop-suffix polynomial coefficients ($d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$). Content fields give the payload kind and size and one digest over the setpoint payload and the sidecar. A variable-length setpoint payload and immutable provenance/assumption sidecar are outside the fixed header, and the MCU verifies their digest before the admission check of @sec-planning-behavior-seam. The payload digest binds content, and the parent digest binds lineage. The record carries no keyed tag, because the permission path admits a proposal by its content rather than its origin (@sec-nervous-cadences).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ **Byte layout:** The trajectory record's field offsets and sizes are given in @sec-appendix-systems-wire-trajectory.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-record-trace
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FILLED TRAJECTORY RECORD FOR THE REACH TOWARD THE MUG
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-trajectory-contract (filled record paragraph).
# │
# │ Goal:    Gather the worked record's field values from the cells that own
# │          them and add the one sidecar value no earlier cell holds.
# │ Show:    3 kg payload bound; 16 x 20 ms = 320 ms nominal end.
# │ How:     RM arm payload capacity; the other fields read
# │          PlanningLeaseRule, PlanningArmTimeline, and PlanningC2Stop.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import kilogram
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_mass

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PlanningRecordTrace:
    """Sidecar payload bound for the worked trajectory record."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    m_payload = RM.arm.payload_capacity  # category: datasheet; arm payload capacity, registry

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_nominal = (PlanningArmTimeline.n_horizon * PlanningArmTimeline.t_period).to(PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp.units)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(m_payload.to(kilogram).magnitude - 3.0) < 1e-9, "arm payload capacity changed")
    check(t_nominal == PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp, "nominal end disagrees with horizon x period")
    check(PlanningLeaseRule.lease_total <= PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear, "lease-path stop no longer inside the clearance")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    m_payload_str = fmt_mass(m_payload, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
```

Filled in for the mug reach, the running record retains the illustrative geometric endpoints of the longer-lease comparison but is superseded or stopped under the shorter operating lease. Its parent is the mug's intent lease, bound by digest; its frame is the machine's base frame, and every time field is in the MCU monotonic clock. Measured from $t_{\mathrm{start}}$, the timing fields hold the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit_str` commitment, the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp_str` nominal end that `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.n_horizon_str` setpoints at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_period_str` give, and the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_end_str` stop end; the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_blend_str` blend target belongs to the alternate schedule, not the operating renewal cadence or the fixed header. The seam fields hold a `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_arm_stop_str` $C^2$ suffix that peaks at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_arm_peak_str` and brings the arm to rest from its `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_arm_str` TCP limit in `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_stop_dist_str`. While the record is in force, the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` chunk lease bounds its tracking, a lapse leads to the state-matched fallback along a path that uses `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.lease_total_str` of the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear_str` clearance. The separate `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` cutoff belongs to the alternate schedule's origin and later clearance check; it grants no extension of the running lease. The sidecar declares a payload of at most `{python} PlanningRecordTrace.m_payload_str`, free space until the grasp, and a scene inside the target ODD. Each field is one the permission path checks at admission or monitors on every tick, without asking the planner what it meant.

In the worked case the deadlines satisfy $t_{\mathrm{start}}\le t_{\mathrm{commit}}<t_{\mathrm{plan\_exp}}<t_{\mathrm{stop\_end}}$. The MCU applies these deadlines under the TRACK and STOP rules of @sec-planning-handoff, and a header timestamp cannot make a mismatched suffix safe. A log records evidence, request, validation, admission, activation, transfer, and stop-completion times in a common converted domain so actual response delay can be measured.

Every record in the runtime chain, from the observation contract through the belief record and the intent lease to the trajectory record itself, now names what it rests on and when it expires. The trajectory record proves only what the planner could foresee, a stop feasible from the states reachable before commitment under the scene and load in its sidecar. Several of the fallacies that follow mistake that bounded proof for a broader one.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-planning-fallacies-pitfalls}

A trajectory remains feasible only while its physical assumptions hold at chunk boundaries and during fallback. Admission and execution checks must address those transitions as well as the nominal path.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Static admission checks protect a machine against obstacle displacements during active execution.*

**Static geometry is an admission precondition, not an execution certificate; dynamic reality always requires runtime monitoring.** The arm begins an admitted reach toward the mug with the conveyor guard clear of its swept volume. During execution, a coworker slides a tote into the tool's path. The admission check was correct for the earlier geometry but no longer supports continued motion. Execution monitoring\index{Execution monitoring!collision detection} must detect the changed clearance and begin deceleration while sufficient stopping room remains. The design must bound how quickly workspace changes become visible via sensor bus latency\index{Network!bus latency} and reserve the stopping margin needed to respond before the updated geometry becomes impossible to avoid.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Couple host spatial screening to bounded, qualified local clearance evidence consumed by the MCU; allocate its refresh latency and memory explicitly. If an unmodeled obstacle breaches the reserved spatial margin $\epsilon_{\text{pos}}$, immediately abort nominal tracking and initiate the validated state-matched fallback.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Checking each action chunk alone without examining the motion the chunks compose.*

**Individual chunk feasibility does not imply composed trajectory stability; stochastic neural chatter can overstress a transmission.** When sequence models (such as diffusion policies or transformers) are sampled stochastically, successive chunks can exhibit high-frequency directional reversals or boundary acceleration mismatches. While every individual chunk satisfies kinematic position and velocity bounds, their concatenation produces rapid torque reversals $\Delta\tau = J_{\text{eff}} \Delta\ddot{q}$. Amplified by reflected rotor inertia ($N_g^2 J_{\text{rotor}}$), this chatter can excite identified flexible modes, increase transmission wear, and add Joule heating ($I^2R$)\index{Motor!Joule heating} in stator windings. Admission must evaluate derivative continuity across each seam, enforce $C^2$ quintic smoothing, and retain motion history to reject oscillating chunk sequences before they excite mechanical modes.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Enforce multi-chunk frequency and reversal monitoring across the execution window. Reject sequences whose spectrum or repeated effort exceeds the identified mechanical or thermal envelope. An antiresonance is a response zero, not a resonant peak. If filtering changes a candidate, repeat the full trajectory, seam, and stop checks before admission.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Delaying fallback transition past the hard stopping horizon in the hope that delayed compute finishes.*

**An overdue compute cycle never justifies extending a physical commitment deadline. Hope is not a deceleration profile.** In the alternate schedule with its `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` admission cutoff, the worked arm's record ends its nominal setpoints at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp_str` and carries a `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_str` matched stop suffix that must finish by `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_end_str`, so the MCU must dispatch fallback\index{Fallback trajectory!commitment point} by `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` to achieve physical onset at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit_str` unless it has admitted a valid replacement. At that point the application processor reports inference nearly complete, but it has not delivered an executable plan. Waiting spends the runway reserved for deceleration. The MCU must follow the matched stop suffix at the commitment point. Progress reports cannot extend a mechanical stopping budget; only a newly validated trajectory can justify continued execution.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Bind the commitment deadline $t_{\mathrm{commit}}$ strictly to the MCU monotonic hardware timer. Close replacement admission and dispatch the resident stop early enough to meet physical onset at commitment, ignoring host progress updates.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Relying solely on feedforward dynamic models when physical contact or payload mass can change abruptly.*

**Feedforward model inversion without closed-loop disturbance bounds turns payload loss into explosive runaway.** The arm lifts an item near its `{python} PlanningRecordTrace.m_payload_str` payload bound using feedforward torque\index{Feedforward control!torque demand} computed for the loaded arm. The item slips from the gripper, but the drives keep applying the same lifting torque to the now unloaded arm, so it accelerates upward. The admitted trajectory has not changed; the dynamics that made its commands appropriate have. Feedback monitoring\index{Feedback control!error monitoring} must detect the resulting tracking error and constrain the commands within the available margin before a mechanical limit strike or thermal derating\index{Motor!thermal derating}. A feedforward model improves nominal tracking, but it cannot replace runtime checks for abrupt changes in payload or contact.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Implement real-time torque and tracking error monitoring ($\|\mathbf{x}_{\text{actual}} - \mathbf{x}_{\text{ref}}\| \le \epsilon_{\text{track}}$) at the 1 kHz servo layer. If sudden payload detachment or contact mismatch causes acceleration to spike, clamp motor currents and transition to compliance or emergency stop.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *A trajectory can omit an achievable terminal stopping suffix if replacement plans are expected to arrive in time.*

**A trajectory without a pre-latched stopping continuation is an unhedged bet on infinite compute availability.** At its `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_drive_str` drive limit, the mobile manipulator's base uses the selected $C^2$ suffix of $T=1.5v_c/a_{\text{brake}}$, `{python} PlanningC2Stop.c2_drive_time_str` at the credible `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_brake_str`, to stop without exceeding that deceleration.\index{Trajectory!braking time} A proposed suffix sized by the constant-deceleration time $v_c/a_{\text{brake}}$ is a third shorter, so its profile peaks at $1.5a_{\text{brake}}$, past what the loaded rack tolerates. Expecting the next plan to arrive does not make this fallback executable. The admission gate must check $T_{\mathrm{stop}} \ge 1.5\,v_c/a_{\text{brake}}$ and certify $d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$ for this selected polynomial profile, rejecting any record that fails. Every accepted trajectory needs a physically certified termination path\index{Fallback trajectory!achievability} for the inevitable occasion when an inference pass is delayed.

**Architect's countermeasure**: For this polynomial stop family, require every candidate trajectory record to include complete, closed-form $C^2$ stopping coefficients satisfying $T_{\mathrm{stop}} \ge 1.5 v_c / a_{\text{brake}}$ and $d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$ within verified clearance. Reject any record at the admission gate that lacks this certified, independently executable return ticket.

:::

## Summary {#sec-planning-summary}

The mug reach can progress through renewed, checked prefixes without forcing the overall task into one observation window. Prediction provides candidate motion; fresh evidence, timely admission, and the current state determine how much may execute. A delayed replacement calls on the resident fallback, so latency-tail targets describe expected service interruption under the fallback premises rather than physical failure by themselves.

The running machine's `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` lease stops a stalled proposal stream through a state-matched response, leaving an illustrative `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.lease_margin_str` before sensing and model uncertainty. The alternate longer-lease case teaches a different limit: replacement admission closes by `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` to permit physical stop onset at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit_str`. Both cases preserve the same obligation to reserve response travel and the entire stop. On the base, the selected smooth profile raises the drive-limit stopping budget to `{python} PlanningC2Stop.total_new_str`, beyond the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_clear_str` rack-end clearance, making the runtime speed decision unavoidable.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Timed motion and independent stopping"}

* **Prediction is not execution authority**: A long predicted path can support short, repeatedly checked prefixes. Renewal cadence determines request throughput; target evidence retains its own capture-based age.
* **Reserve a response from the current state**: The matched suffix belongs to its declared entry state. Earlier lease or evidence expiry needs a validated state-matched fallback, available sensing and drive energy, and enough clearance for response delay plus stopping.
* **Admission precedes physical commitment**: The alternate arm schedule closes admission by `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` to begin its stop at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit_str`. A late proposer cannot spend that response interval.
* **Smoothness still needs feasibility checks**: Six boundary conditions determine the quintic seam, but its interior jerk, torque, and clearance decide whether that seam can execute.
* **A gentle stop can cost more distance**: The selected cruise-entry profile travels half again the constant-deceleration distance at the same peak. That factor belongs to this profile and drives the base's remaining speed restriction.
* **Rejecting a candidate need not stop service**: The current record can continue while its own state, evidence, lease, and fallback remain valid. A rejected replacement renews none of them.
* **Admission and enforcement need separate budgets**: Whole-plan validation scans bounded candidate content; per-tick permission checks current state and local evidence. Their execution time, memory, and interference must be allocated separately.

:::

The trajectory record joins the decisions made throughout this chapter: when to request a replacement, which motion the body can follow, how to join it to the current state, and when to stop waiting. Its conditions remain live obligations during execution. The permission path must therefore compare the running motion with fresh state and the remaining stopping margin on every tick, even after the complete plan has passed admission.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From admitted plans to per-tick permission"}
This chapter admits whole proposals. The MCU checks a complete trajectory and its matched stop before the admission cutoff and latches the stop in protected memory. Admission judges the plan against a reachable state envelope, and activation checks the current estimate against that envelope, yet while the plan runs the plant can lag its reference, an obstacle can appear, and an actuator can saturate. @Sec-enforcement checks each tick against live state, insets the stopping distance by the tracking error the controller can bound, and owns the fallback ladder whose stop rung plays this chapter's resident stop. That inset completes the spatial terms accounted for here and yields a candidate aisle speed. Operating permission still requires complete capture-to-admission timing, positive stopping reserve, and qualification of the response under the declared conditions.
:::
